notes: BATCH_005 Banking and Financial Awareness part: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) across 32 topics, IDs BANK_BFA_000804 to BANK_BFA_001003. Built mostly from primary texts opened on 2026-11-05: RBI history chronologies (1935-2003) and table of Bank Rate/CRR/SLR changes; RBI Organisation page; RBI FAQs on Indian currency, cheque clearing, RBI as banker to Government, SGBs, non-competitive bidding, the G-sec primer, RTGS, NEFT, ARCs, PSL, PPIs, ATMs, the PSS Act, UDGAM, Paytm Payments Bank restrictions, RB-IOS 2026 and the e-rupee; IRAC Directions and the stressed-assets framework; RBI's payments booklet; MPC resolutions and Governor's statements of May 2020, December 2025, February, August and October 2026 and the February 2026 developmental statement; RBI press releases (Bank Rate 2012, RTGS 24x7, payments bank and SFB guidelines 2014, NBFC-UL list 2026-27, CVA directions, lending rates, VRRR and T-bill results of November 2026, TCCFM); October 2026 notifications on leverage ratio, operational risk and NDDCs; PIB Budget 2026-27 summary and PMJDY 12-year note; DFS PMJJBY page; SIDBI ecosystem page; Insurance Ombudsman FAQs; SEBI board meeting of 24 September 2026 and SEBI investor pages. Facts available only through search results (NPCI circulars, some news-only facts; no block was worked around) are marked web:search-confirmed. Only changeable values and dated events carry current_affairs, with the event or release date from the source. Computed answers are re-derived in tools/batch_005/banking.py. Facts tested in BATCH_000-BATCH_004 are not repeated. ai:independent-check marks only the questions a separate fresh solver answered blind and got right.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Separate clearing sessions for non-CTS cheques were discontinued with effect from 31 December 2018. According to RBI, what is the status of a non-CTS cheque today?

options.text: It cannot be presented in CTS clearing but remains valid as a negotiable instrument
It is void and cannot be used for any purpose
It can be cleared only through a separate weekly session
It can be presented in CTS if the drawer counter-signs it

solution.explanation: Banks were advised to issue only CTS-2010 compliant cheques from 30 September 2012, and separate clearing sessions for non-CTS cheques ended on 31 December 2018. Non-CTS cheques cannot be presented in CTS, but such a cheque continues to be valid as a negotiable instrument.
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI does not call them void; no weekly session or counter-signature route exists.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It cannot be presented in CTS clearing but remains valid as a negotiable instrument

fact_checks.claim: Separate clearing sessions for non-CTS cheques were discontinued with effect from December 31, 2018; non-CTS cheques cannot be presented in CTS; however, a non-CTS cheque continues to be valid as a negotiable instrument

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: With effect from 13 October 2023, the three CTS grids (New Delhi, Chennai and Mumbai) were merged into a National Grid. Where is the National Grid Clearing House (NGCH) that manages it?

solution.explanation: RBI's cheque-clearing FAQs state that the three CTS grids were merged with effect from 13 October 2023 to form a National Grid managed by the National Grid Clearing House (NGCH), Chennai.
solution.why_others_wrong: Mumbai and New Delhi were earlier grid locations, not the NGCH; Nagpur houses RBI's Central Accounts Section.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Chennai

fact_checks.claim: With effect from October 13, 2023, the three grids were merged to form a National Grid managed by National Grid Clearing House (NGCH), Chennai

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Cheque Truncation System the physical cheque stays with the presenting bank. For how long must the presenting bank preserve the physical instruments to meet legal requirements?

solution.explanation: Physical cheques do not move to the paying bank under CTS. To meet legal requirements, the presenting banks that truncate the cheques must preserve the physical instruments for 10 years.
steps: Truncated cheque stays with presenting bank
solution.why_others_wrong: 3, 5 and 8 years are not the period stated by RBI.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 10 years

fact_checks.claim: To meet legal requirements, the presenting banks, which truncate the cheques, need to preserve the physical instruments for a period of 10 years

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which law, which came into force on 12 January 1984, provided nomination facilities to bank account holders for the first time and also widened the activities banks could undertake, such as leasing?

options.text: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970

solution.concept: Origin of nomination in bank accounts
solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 1983, which came into force on 12 January 1984, widened banks' activities (such as leasing), provided nomination facilities to account holders and strengthened RBI's powers.
solution.why_others_wrong: The 1949 Act is the base law; the 1970 Act nationalised banks; the 1961 Act set up deposit insurance.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 1983

fact_checks.claim: 12 Jan 1984: Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 1983 widened the activities that banks could undertake (such as leasing), provided nomination facilities to account holders, strengthened the powers of the Reserve Bank

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A savings account holder of Bank A uses ATMs of other banks in Hyderabad. Under RBI's ATM rules, how many free transactions in a month must Bank A at least allow him at these other-bank ATMs?

options.text: Five financial transactions, with non-financial ones free
Five, including financial and non-financial transactions
Three, including financial and non-financial transactions

solution.explanation: At other banks' ATMs in the six metro locations (Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, New Delhi), banks must offer at least three free transactions a month, financial and non-financial together. At non-metro locations the minimum is five; at the bank's own ATMs it is five free financial transactions.
steps: Hyderabad is one of the six metro locations
Off-us at metro → minimum 3 free (financial + non-financial)
solution.why_others_wrong: Five applies to non-metro off-us ATMs or own-bank ATMs; free use is not unlimited.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Three, including financial and non-financial transactions

fact_checks.claim: In case of ATMs located in six metro locations, viz. Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, and New Delhi, banks shall offer their savings bank account holders a minimum of three free transactions (including financial and non-financial transactions) in a month

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer's account is debited for an ATM cash withdrawal, but no cash is dispensed. Within what maximum time must the card-issuing bank re-credit the account, as per RBI?

options.text: T+5 calendar days, where T is the day of the transaction

solution.explanation: Banks must reverse failed ATM/WLA transactions on their own; RBI has mandated that the customer's account be re-credited within a maximum of T+5 calendar days.
solution.why_others_wrong: T+1, 30 days and 90 days are not the prescribed limit.
solution.final_answer: Option C: T+5 calendar days, where T is the day of the transaction

fact_checks.claim: In the case of a failed ATM transaction, the banks have been mandated to re-credit the customer's account within a maximum of T+5 calendar days (where 'T' is the day of transaction)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer has written the wrong amount in words on a cheque. Under the Cheque Truncation System, what should she do?

options.text: Use a fresh cheque leaf, because cheques with alterations are not accepted in CTS
Strike out the words and countersign the change
Write the correction on the back and sign it
Ask the bank to correct it after scanning

solution.explanation: RBI's cheque-clearing FAQs say cheques with alterations are not accepted under CTS. Apart from date validation, no change can be made; for a change in payee name, amount in figures or amount in words, a fresh cheque leaf must be used.
solution.why_others_wrong: Countersigned or back-side corrections and post-scan correction are not permitted.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Use a fresh cheque leaf, because cheques with alterations are not accepted in CTS

fact_checks.claim: Cheques with alteration / modification are not accepted under CTS; no changes / corrections can be carried out on the cheques (other than for date validation purposes); for any change in the payee's name, courtesy amount or legal amount, fresh cheque leaves should be used

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's chronology, an Ordinance of July 1981 barred companies, co-operative societies and firms from repaying any deposit of ₹10,000 or more otherwise than by:

options.text: An account payee cheque or bank draft

solution.concept: Repayment of deposits through banking channels
solution.explanation: The July 1981 Ordinance prohibited companies (including banking companies), co-operative societies and firms from repaying any deposit otherwise than by an account payee cheque or bank draft when the repayment amounted to ₹10,000 or more.
steps: Repayment ≥ ₹10,000 → account payee cheque / bank draft only
solution.why_others_wrong: Cash, bearer cheques and money orders were exactly what the rule sought to avoid.
solution.final_answer: Option B: An account payee cheque or bank draft

fact_checks.claim: 11 July 1981: Ordinance prohibiting companies (including Banking Companies), cooperative societies, firms, to repay any person any deposit otherwise than by an account payee cheque / bank draft when such repayment amounted to Rs. 10,000 or more

options.text: Small Industries Development Bank of India

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In one month, a savings account holder of Bank X in Chennai makes 6 cash withdrawals at Bank X's own ATMs and 5 transactions (cash withdrawals and balance enquiries) at other banks' ATMs in Chennai. Assuming Bank X allows only the minimum free transactions and charges the maximum permitted fee, what is the most it can charge (excluding taxes)?

solution.explanation: At its own ATMs a bank must allow at least five free financial transactions a month, so the sixth withdrawal is chargeable. At other banks' ATMs in a metro (Chennai), the minimum is three free transactions including non-financial ones, so two of the five are chargeable. The charge cannot exceed ₹23 per transaction: 3 × ₹23 = ₹69.
steps: Other-bank ATM in metro: 5 − 3 free = 2 chargeable
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹46 ignores the sixth own-ATM withdrawal; ₹23 counts only one chargeable transaction; ₹115 charges all five other-bank ATM transactions.
solution.final_answer: Option C: ₹69

fact_checks.claim: Banks should offer their savings bank account holders a minimum of five free financial transactions in a month at own ATMs; minimum of three free transactions at other banks' ATMs in six metro locations; charges cannot exceed a maximum of Rs. 23 per transaction (plus applicable taxes)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the Cheque Truncation System, as described in RBI's FAQs of January 2026:
I. Three images of each cheque are captured: front grey scale, front black-and-white and back black-and-white.
II. RBI has prescribed specific ink colours that customers must use to write cheques.
III. Under continuous clearing, presenting banks release the payment to customers within one hour of successful settlement, subject to usual safeguards.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: CTS captures three images of each cheque (I correct). Customers should use image-friendly, permanent ink, but RBI has not prescribed specific ink colours (II wrong). Under continuous clearing, after settlement the presenting bank releases payment within one hour, subject to usual safeguards (III correct).
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option including II is wrong; 'I only' omits III.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: There are three images of each cheque that are taken in CTS – front Gray Scale, front Black and White and back Black and White; RBI has not prescribed specific ink colours to be used to write cheques
Presenting banks will release the payment to the customers within one hour of the successful settlement, subject to usual safeguard

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 made banks of erstwhile princely states subsidiaries of SBI. Which statement about these banks is correct?

options.text: The Bank of Bikaner and the Bank of Jaipur were amalgamated in 1963 to form the State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur
The Bank of Mysore and the Bank of Travancore were amalgamated in 1963 to form the State Bank of Mysore
The Bank of Patiala and the Bank of Indore were amalgamated in 1963 to form the State Bank of Patiala
Only three banks became subsidiaries under the 1959 Act

solution.explanation: Under the 1959 Act, the Bank of Bikaner, Bank of Jaipur, Bank of Indore, Bank of Mysore, Bank of Patiala, Bank of Hyderabad, Bank of Saurashtra and Bank of Travancore became SBI subsidiaries. The Bank of Bikaner and the Bank of Jaipur were amalgamated in 1963 to form the State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur.
steps: 1963 → Bikaner + Jaipur = State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur
solution.why_others_wrong: No 1963 merger of Mysore with Travancore or Patiala with Indore took place; eight, not three, banks were made subsidiaries.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Bank of Bikaner and the Bank of Jaipur were amalgamated in 1963 to form the State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur

fact_checks.claim: State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959 made the banks of the erstwhile Princely States subsidiaries of SBI (Bikaner, Jaipur, Indore, Mysore, Patiala, Hyderabad, Saurashtra, Travancore); the Bank of Bikaner and the Bank of Jaipur were amalgamated in 1963 to form the State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The 14 banks nationalised on 19 July 1969 were Indian scheduled commercial banks with deposits of over:

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that the 14 major Indian scheduled commercial banks with deposits of over ₹50 crore were nationalised on 19 July 1969.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹200 crore relates to the 1980 round; ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore are not the 1969 threshold.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹50 crore

fact_checks.claim: 19 Jul 1969: 14 major Indian Scheduled Commercial Banks with deposits of over Rs 50 crores nationalised

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 10 February 1970 the Supreme Court held the 1969 bank nationalisation law void. How was nationalisation then given effect?

options.text: A fresh Ordinance on 14 February 1970, later replaced by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970
By an amendment to the RBI Act, 1934 transferring the banks to RBI
By a constitutional amendment passed in 1972
The banks were returned to private owners until 1980

solution.explanation: The Supreme Court found the Act discriminatory against the 14 banks and the compensation unfair. A fresh Ordinance was issued on 14 February 1970 and later replaced by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 (5 of 1970).
solution.why_others_wrong: Nationalisation was not routed through the RBI Act, a 1972 constitutional amendment or a reversal.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A fresh Ordinance on 14 February 1970, later replaced by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970

fact_checks.claim: On February 10, 1970 the Supreme Court held the Act void; a fresh Ordinance was issued on February 14 which was later replaced by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Before the 1969 nationalisation, the Government introduced 'social controls' over banks in December 1967. Which body was set up on 22 December 1967 as a forum to assess credit priorities on an all-India basis?

solution.explanation: Social controls were introduced in December 1967 to align banking with economic policy. The National Credit Council, set up on 22 December 1967, was a forum to discuss and assess credit priorities and to assist RBI and the Government in allocating credit.
solution.why_others_wrong: The Agricultural Credit Board came in 1970, SLBCs in 1971 and the Banks Board Bureau in 2016.
solution.final_answer: Option B: National Credit Council

fact_checks.claim: Dec 1967: Introduction of Social Controls over banks; 22 Dec 1967: National Credit Council set up to provide a forum to discuss and assess credit priorities on an all India basis

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: From 1960, RBI acquired powers for reconstruction and compulsory amalgamation of weak banks. According to RBI's chronology, roughly how many banks were merged or liquidated between 1960 and 1982?

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology says the policy of reconstruction/compulsory amalgamation introduced in 1960 (with powers acquired through an RBI Act amendment) led to over 200 banks being merged or liquidated between 1960 and 1982.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 is the number nationalised in 1969; 50 and 1,000 do not match the record.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Over 200

fact_checks.claim: 1960: Policy of reconstruction / compulsory amalgamation of banks introduced to consolidate the Banking sector; between 1960 to 1982 over 200 banks were merged or liquidated

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Banking Commission set up on 29 January 1969 was asked to report on banking costs, legislation affecting banking, indigenous banking, bank procedures and non-banking financial intermediaries.
II. Recommendations made in April 1998 on harmonising the roles of development financial institutions and banks paved the way for universal banking in India.
III. The Banking Commission of 1969 was constituted by RBI under the Banking Regulation Act.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The Banking Commission of 29 January 1969 had the terms of reference in I, but it was set up by the Government of India, not RBI (III wrong). RBI's chronology records that the April 1998 recommendations on harmonising the roles of DFIs and banks paved the way for universal banking (II).
solution.why_others_wrong: III is wrong, so any option including it fails; 'I only' omits II.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: 29 Jan 1969: Setting up of the Banking Commission by GOI to report on banking costs, legislations affecting banking, indigenous banking, bank procedures, non banking financial intermediaries
Apr 1998: Recommendations on the harmonisation of the Role and Operations of Development Financial Institutions and Banks paved the way for universal banking in India

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Who was the Governor of RBI at that time?

solution.explanation: Sir C. D. Deshmukh assumed office on 11 August 1943. RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949, and Sir Benegal Rama Rau took over only on 1 July 1949, so Deshmukh was Governor at nationalisation.
solution.why_others_wrong: Rama Rau came after July 1949, Taylor before 1943 and Iengar in 1957.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Sir C. D. Deshmukh

fact_checks.claim: 11 Aug 1943: Sir C. D. Deshmukh assumes office of Governor; 1 Jan 1949: Reserve Bank of India nationalised; 1 Jul 1949: Sir Benegal Rama Rau assumes office as Governor

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Who was appointed Governor of RBI on 22 November 1997, shortly before RBI responded to the Asian currency crisis?

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that Bimal Jalan was appointed Governor on 22 November 1997; a series of measures in response to the Asian currency crisis followed on 28 November 1997.
solution.why_others_wrong: Rangarajan took over in 1992, Venkitaramanan in 1990, and Reddy succeeded Jalan in 2003.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Bimal Jalan

fact_checks.claim: 22 Nov 1997: Bimal Jalan appointed Governor; 28 Nov 1997: a series of measures introduced in response to the Asian Currency Crisis

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: From 1937, RBI performed central banking roles for a neighbouring territory. Which?

options.text: It acted as banker to the Government of Burma and was responsible for note issue in Burma
It acted as banker to the Government of Nepal
It managed the public debt of Afghanistan

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that in 1937 RBI acted as banker to the Government of Burma and was responsible for note issue in Burma. In 1945 it was also entrusted with the currency and coinage of the British Military Administration of Burma.
steps: 1937 → banker to Burma Government + note issue in Burma
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI had no such role for Ceylon, Nepal or Afghanistan.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It acted as banker to the Government of Burma and was responsible for note issue in Burma

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: N. C. Sengupta was Governor of RBI only from 19 May 1975 to 19 August 1975. Who was appointed Governor on 20 August 1975?

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records N. C. Sengupta as Governor up to 19 August 1975 and K. R. Puri's appointment on 20 August 1975. M. Narasimham followed in May 1977 and I. G. Patel in December 1977.
solution.why_others_wrong: Jagannathan preceded Sengupta; Narasimham and Patel came in 1977.
solution.final_answer: Option D: K. R. Puri

questions.question_text: Which person served as RBI Governor for only about six weeks in 1970, between L. K. Jha and S. Jagannathan?

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that B. N. Adarkar was appointed Governor on 4 May 1970 till 15 June, and S. Jagannathan was appointed on 16 June 1970.
solution.why_others_wrong: Bhattacharyya served from 1962, Ambegaonkar briefly in 1957 and Sengupta in 1975.
solution.final_answer: Option A: B. N. Adarkar

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following developments in RBI's organisation:
I. A Department of Banking Development was created in October 1950 together with the new post of Executive Director.
II. The RBI (Amendment) Act, 1951 enabled RBI to become banker to Part B States after executing agreements with them.
III. An Urban Banks Department was formed on 1 February 1984 to supervise urban co-operative banks.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: All three are recorded in RBI's chronology: the Department of Banking Development and the post of Executive Director (October 1950), banker to Part B States under the 1951 amendment, and the Urban Banks Department (1 February 1984).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options leaves out a correct statement.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I, II and III

fact_checks.claim: Oct 1950: Department of Banking Development created together with the new post of Executive Director; 1951: RBI (Amendment) Act, 1951 enabled the Bank to become Banker to Part B states after executing agreements with them
01 Feb 1984: Urban Banks Department formed to supervise the affairs of Urban Cooperative Banks

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI pays its Central Board directors a sitting fee of ₹60,000 per Central Board meeting and ₹30,000 per meeting of the Committee of the Central Board (CCB), plus a halting allowance of ₹3,750 per day. A director attends 3 Board meetings and 4 CCB meetings and is eligible for 5 days of halting allowance in a year. What does RBI pay as sitting fees and halting allowance (travel and stay are borne separately)?

solution.concept: Remuneration of RBI's Central Board directors
solution.explanation: Sitting fees: 3 × ₹60,000 = ₹1,80,000 and 4 × ₹30,000 = ₹1,20,000. Halting allowance: 5 × ₹3,750 = ₹18,750. Total = ₹3,18,750. Travel and stay expenses are borne by RBI in addition.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,00,000 omits the halting allowance; ₹2,58,750 pays CCB meetings at half the actual count; ₹4,38,750 pays CCB meetings at the Board rate.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ₹3,18,750

fact_checks.claim: Sitting fees per meeting: Central Board ₹60,000; Committee of the Central Board ₹30,000; halting allowance per diem ₹3,750; travel and stay expenses are also borne by the Reserve Bank

questions.question_text: Apart from Hindi in the centre and English on the reverse, how many languages appear in the language panel of Indian banknotes?

solution.explanation: RBI's currency FAQs state that fifteen languages appear in the language panel of banknotes, in addition to Hindi in the centre and English on the reverse.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22 is the number of Eighth Schedule languages, not those on the panel; 12 and 18 are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 15

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: With effect from 30 June 2011, coins of which denomination were withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender?

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs state that 25 paise coins were withdrawn from circulation with effect from 30 June 2011; coins below 25 paise had been withdrawn much earlier. 50 paise and higher coins remain legal tender.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 paise and ₹1 coins remain legal tender; 10 paise was withdrawn earlier, not alongside a continuing 25 paise coin.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 25 paise

fact_checks.claim: Twenty-five (25) paise coins have been withdrawn from circulation with effect from June 30, 2011 and are no more legal tender; coins of denominations below 25 paise were withdrawn much earlier

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under which section of the RBI Act, 1934 is RBI obliged to undertake the receipts and payments of the Central Government and to manage the public debt of the Union?

solution.concept: Statutory basis of banker to Government
solution.explanation: Section 20 places on RBI the obligation to undertake the receipts and payments of the Central Government and to carry out its exchange, remittance and banking operations, including management of the public debt. Section 21 gives RBI the right to transact the Union's business.
solution.why_others_wrong: Section 17 lists RBI's business, Section 45 deals with agency banks and Section 42 with CRR.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Section 20

fact_checks.claim: In terms of Section 20 of the RBI Act 1934, RBI has the obligation to undertake the receipts and payments of the Central Government and to carry out the exchange, remittance and other banking operations, including the management of the public debt of the Union

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the RBI (Note Refund) Rules as amended in 2018, a mutilated ₹500 note is paid full value only if the area of its single largest undivided piece is:

solution.explanation: For notes of ₹50 and above, the 2018 amendment pays full value if the largest undivided piece is more than 80%, half value if it is 40% to 80%, and nothing below 40%. The earlier (2009) full-value threshold was 65%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 65% was the pre-2018 threshold; 50% applies to notes up to ₹20; 40% is the half-value floor.
solution.final_answer: Option A: More than 80% of the note

fact_checks.claim: Notes of ₹50 and above (amended NRR 2018): area less than 40% – reject; 40% to 80% – half value; single largest undivided piece more than 80% – full value

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI pays agency banks a commission for conducting Government business. At the rates applicable from 1 July 2019, what does an agency bank earn for a Government receipt collected in e-mode?

solution.explanation: The agency commission rates are ₹40 per physical receipt, ₹9 per e-mode receipt, ₹75 per pension payment and 6.5 paise per ₹100 of turnover for payments other than pension.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹40 is for physical receipts, ₹75 for pension payments, and 6.5 paise per ₹100 for other payments.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ₹9 per transaction

fact_checks.claim: Agency commission from July 1, 2019: Receipts – physical mode ₹40 per transaction; Receipts – e-mode ₹9 per transaction; Payments – pension ₹75 per transaction; Payments other than pension 6.5 paise per ₹100 turnover

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which designates RBI as the authority to regulate and supervise payment systems, came into force on:

solution.concept: Legal basis of payment system oversight
solution.explanation: The PSS Act received the President's assent on 20 December 2007 and came into force on 12 August 2008, the same date as the Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations, 2008.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 December 2007 is the assent date; 1 April 2008 is wrong; 14 December 2020 is when RTGS became 24x7.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 12 August 2008

fact_checks.claim: The PSS Act, 2007 received the assent of the President on 20th December 2007 and it came into force with effect from 12th August 2008

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper brings three mutilated ₹500 notes to a bank branch. The single largest undivided piece of each is 85%, 60% and 35% of the note respectively. Under the Note Refund Rules as amended in 2018, how much will he receive?

solution.explanation: For ₹50 and above: more than 80% → full value; 40%–80% → half value; below 40% → rejected. So ₹500 + ₹250 + 0 = ₹750.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,000 pays the 60% note in full; ₹1,250 also pays the 35% note at half value; ₹500 pays nothing for the 60% note.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹750

fact_checks.claim: Notes of ₹50 and above: less than 40% – reject; 40% to 80% – half value; more than 80% – full value (Note Refund Rules as amended in 2018)

At the agency commission rates in force since 1 July 2019, what commission does RBI pay it?

solution.explanation: Physical receipts 1,000 × ₹40 = ₹40,000; e-mode receipts 5,000 × ₹9 = ₹45,000; pension 200 × ₹75 = ₹15,000; other payments ₹50 crore ÷ 100 × 6.5 paise = ₹3,25,000. Total = ₹4,25,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,00,000 omits the turnover commission; ₹3,65,000 omits the e-mode and pension commission; ₹3,40,000 counts only pension and turnover commission.
solution.final_answer: Option A: ₹4,25,000

fact_checks.claim: Agency commission from July 1, 2019: physical receipts ₹40; e-mode receipts ₹9; pension payments ₹75 per transaction; payments other than pension 6.5 paise per ₹100 turnover

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In his statement of 5 December 2025, the RBI Governor clarified the primary purpose of open market operations (OMOs). What is it?

options.text: To set the policy repo rate
To provide sufficient (durable) liquidity, not to directly influence G-sec yields
To directly target the 10-year G-sec yield
To manage the exchange rate of the rupee

solution.explanation: The Governor reiterated that the policy repo rate is the primary instrument of monetary policy and that the primary purpose of OMOs is to provide sufficient liquidity, not to directly influence G-sec yields.
steps: OMOs → liquidity provision, not yield targeting

solution.final_answer: Option B: To provide sufficient (durable) liquidity, not to directly influence G-sec yields

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In December 2025 RBI bought government securities through OMOs and, at the same time, absorbed funds through VRRR auctions. How did the Governor explain this?

options.text: OMOs are meant to raise G-sec yields while VRRRs lower them
The two operations cancel out and have no purpose
OMOs manage durable liquidity while repo/VRRR operations manage transient liquidity to keep the WACR near the repo rate
VRRRs are used only for exchange rate management

solution.explanation: The Governor said OMO purchases (sales) provide (absorb) durable liquidity, while short-term LAF operations (VRR/VRRR) manage transient liquidity to align the WACR with the repo rate. solution.why_others_wrong: OMOs are not meant to move yields; the operations serve different purposes; VRRRs are not FX tools.

It narrowed by 4 bps, from 2.94 to 2.90 percentage points

How did the average WACR move between the two periods?

options.text: From 6 bps below the repo rate to 14 bps above it, a rise of about 20 bps
It fell by about 8 bps, to about 5.23%
From 6 bps above the repo rate to 14 bps below it, a fall of about 20 bps (to about 5.11%)
It stayed at the repo rate in both periods

solution.why_others_wrong: The direction in the second option is reversed; 8 bps subtracts 6 from 14; the WACR was not at the repo rate.
solution.final_answer: Option C: From 6 bps above the repo rate to 14 bps below it, a fall of about 20 bps (to about 5.11%)

As the new policy rate replacing the repo rate

Following KYC directions for acquired financial assets

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
A bank reviews three NPAs for erosion in security:
P. Outstanding ₹150 lakh; the realisable value of security is now ₹12 lakh.
Q. Outstanding ₹150 lakh; the realisable value has fallen to 45% of the value assessed at the last inspection, but is still ₹40 lakh.
R. Outstanding ₹100 lakh; the realisable value is 90% of the earlier assessed value.
Under RBI's IRAC norms, how should P and Q be treated?

options.text: P as doubtful asset; Q as loss asset
P straightaway as loss asset; Q straightaway as doubtful asset
Both continue in their normal ageing category

solution.concept: Accelerated classification for erosion of security
solution.explanation: If the realisable value of security is less than 10% of the outstanding, the security is ignored and the asset is straightaway a loss asset: P (12 < 15). If erosion is significant—realisable value below 50% of the value assessed earlier—the NPA may straightaway be classified doubtful: Q (45%). R has no significant erosion.
solution.why_others_wrong: The P/Q treatments are swapped in the second option; Q is not below the 10% test; erosion rules do apply.
solution.final_answer: Option C: P straightaway as loss asset; Q straightaway as doubtful asset

fact_checks.claim: Erosion in the value of security shall be reckoned as significant when the realisable value of the security is less than fifty per cent of the value assessed; such NPAs may be straightaway classified under doubtful category; if the realisable value of the security is less than ten per cent of the outstanding, the asset shall be straightaway classified as loss asset

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A ₹20 lakh MSE loan covered by a CGTMSE guarantee (75% of the unsecured amount) has been doubtful for two years. The realisable value of security is ₹4 lakh. Following RBI's IRAC illustration (40% on the secured portion for 1–3 years doubtful, 100% on the unsecured and uncovered portion, nothing on the guaranteed portion), what provision is required?

solution.explanation: Unsecured = 20 − 4 = ₹16 lakh. CGTMSE cover = 75% × 16 = ₹12 lakh, needing no provision. Unsecured and uncovered = ₹4 lakh at 100% = ₹4 lakh. Secured ₹4 lakh at 40% = ₹1.6 lakh. Total ₹5.6 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹17.6 lakh ignores the guarantee; ₹12.0 lakh provides on the guaranteed part; ₹1.6 lakh covers only the secured portion.
solution.final_answer: Option C: ₹5.6 lakh

fact_checks.claim: In case the advance covered by schemes/guarantees of CGTMSE, CRGFTLIH and NCGTC becomes non-performing, no provision need be made towards the guaranteed portion; illustration: secured portion @ 40 per cent, unsecured and uncovered portion @ 100 per cent
Doubtful assets – secured portion: up to one year 25 per cent; one to three years 40 per cent; more than three years 100 per cent

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: How is the Basel III leverage ratio defined in RBI's capital adequacy directions?

options.text: Capital measure (Tier 1 capital) divided by the exposure measure, expressed as a percentage
Total capital divided by risk-weighted assets
High-quality liquid assets divided by 30-day net outflows
Available stable funding divided by required stable funding

solution.explanation: The leverage ratio is the capital measure (Tier 1 capital) as the numerator divided by the exposure measure as the denominator, expressed as a percentage. It is a non-risk-based backstop to the risk-weighted capital ratio.
solution.why_others_wrong: The others define CRAR, LCR and NSFR respectively.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Capital measure (Tier 1 capital) divided by the exposure measure, expressed as a percentage

fact_checks.claim: The Basel III leverage ratio is defined as the capital measure (the numerator) divided by the exposure measure (the denominator), with this ratio expressed as a percentage; Tier 1 leverage ratio requirement

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's amended leverage ratio framework (October 2026), how is the exposure measure generally computed?

options.text: On risk-weighted values after credit risk mitigation
On net values after netting deposits against loans
On gross accounting values, without using collateral, guarantees or other credit risk mitigation to reduce it and without netting assets and liabilities

solution.explanation: The exposure measure generally follows gross accounting values; unless specified otherwise, a bank shall not take account of physical or financial collateral, guarantees or other CRM to reduce it, and shall not net assets and liabilities.
solution.why_others_wrong: Risk weighting, netting and an off-balance-sheet-only measure are all inconsistent with the rule.
solution.final_answer: Option D: On gross accounting values, without using collateral, guarantees or other credit risk mitigation to reduce it and without netting assets and liabilities

fact_checks.claim: The leverage ratio exposure measure generally follows gross accounting values; a bank shall not take account of physical or financial collateral, guarantees or other credit risk mitigation techniques to reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure and shall not net assets and liabilities

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's October 2026 amendment, what scope of consolidation does the Basel III leverage ratio framework follow?

options.text: The same scope of regulatory consolidation as the risk-based capital framework
Accounting consolidation including insurance subsidiaries in all cases

solution.explanation: The amendment substitutes paragraph 263(1): the leverage ratio framework follows the same scope of regulatory consolidation, including consolidation criteria, as the risk-based capital framework.
solution.why_others_wrong: The rule is not solo-only, branch-only or full accounting consolidation.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The same scope of regulatory consolidation as the risk-based capital framework

fact_checks.claim: The Basel III leverage ratio framework shall follow the same scope of regulatory consolidation, including consolidation criteria, as is used for the risk-based capital framework

For a branch in the first G-SIB bucket (1% buffer), with no countercyclical buffer in force, what CET1 ratio must it meet?

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank's on-balance-sheet assets at gross accounting value are ₹1,00,200 crore. These include a ₹200 crore investment in an unconsolidated financial entity that has been deducted from CET1, leaving Tier 1 capital of ₹3,900 crore. Under RBI's leverage ratio rules (items deducted from Tier 1 are also deducted from the exposure measure), what is its leverage ratio, and how does it fare?

options.text: 3.9%; it meets the minimum even as a D-SIB
3.9%; it meets the 3.5% minimum for other banks but would fall short of the 4% D-SIB minimum

solution.explanation: Exposure measure = 1,00,200 − 200 (deducted from Tier 1) = ₹1,00,000 crore. Leverage ratio = 3,900 / 1,00,000 = 3.9%. That clears the 3.5% minimum for non-D-SIB banks but not the 4% D-SIB minimum.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.89% fails to deduct the ₹200 crore; 3.9% is below the D-SIB 4%; 4.1% is a miscalculation.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 3.9%; it meets the 3.5% minimum for other banks but would fall short of the 4% D-SIB minimum

fact_checks.claim: Any item deducted from Tier 1 capital and regulatory adjustments other than those related to liabilities shall be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure; the minimum leverage ratio for a D-SIB shall be 4 per cent and 3.5 per cent for other banks

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's amendment of 23 October 2026 to its forthcoming operational-risk capital directions (effective 1 April 2027) clarified the treatment of interest rate derivative assets in the 'interest earning assets' used for the Business Indicator. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They are included at notional value
They are included at fair value (not notional), using only positive fair values, without subtracting negative fair values
They are excluded from interest earning assets
They are included at net fair value after offsetting negative values

solution.concept: Business Indicator under the standardised approach for operational risk
solution.explanation: Interest rate derivative assets that affect interest income are included in interest earning assets at fair value, not notional value; the fair value used is positive and a negative fair value is not subtracted.
solution.why_others_wrong: Notional value, exclusion and netting all contradict the amendment.
solution.final_answer: Option B: They are included at fair value (not notional), using only positive fair values, without subtracting negative fair values

solution.explanation: Revenue receipts = net tax revenue + non-tax revenue = 28.67 + 6.66 = ₹35.33 lakh crore. NTR share = 6.66 ÷ 35.33 ≈ 18.9%. (6.66 ÷ 28.67 ≈ 23.2% is NTR relative to net tax, not to receipts.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 23.2% divides by net tax; ₹22.01 lakh crore subtracts; ₹44.04 lakh crore is gross tax revenue.
solution.final_answer: Option A: ₹35.33 lakh crore; about 18.9%

fact_checks.claim: The Tax Revenues (Net to Centre) are projected to be ₹28.67 lakh crore; NTR of the Central Government is projected at ₹6.66 lakh crore; Revenue Receipts estimated at ₹35.33 lakh crore

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In BE 2026-27, gross tax revenue (GTR) is ₹44.04 lakh crore, a growth of 8.0% over RE 2025-26, with direct taxes at ₹26.97 lakh crore and indirect taxes at ₹17.07 lakh crore. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Indirect taxes are about 61.2% of GTR, and RE 2025-26 GTR was about ₹47.6 lakh crore
Direct taxes are about 38.8% of GTR, and RE 2025-26 GTR was about ₹40.8 lakh crore
Direct taxes are about 61.2% of GTR, and RE 2025-26 GTR works out to about ₹40.8 lakh crore
Direct taxes are about 61.2% of GTR, and RE 2025-26 GTR was about ₹47.6 lakh crore

solution.explanation: 26.97 + 17.07 = 44.04; direct share = 26.97 ÷ 44.04 ≈ 61.2%. RE 2025-26 GTR = 44.04 ÷ 1.08 ≈ ₹40.8 lakh crore (₹47.6 lakh crore would wrongly add 8%).
solution.why_others_wrong: Indirect taxes are 38.8%; 47.6 multiplies instead of dividing by 1.08.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Direct taxes are about 61.2% of GTR, and RE 2025-26 GTR works out to about ₹40.8 lakh crore

fact_checks.claim: In BE 2026-27, Gross Tax Revenue (GTR) is estimated at ₹44.04 lakh crore. It represents a growth of 8.0 per cent over RE 2025-26. Direct Taxes at ₹26.97 lakh crore are the major contributor to GTR (61.2 per cent of the GTR). Indirect taxes are estimated at ₹17.07 lakh crore

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the one-time six-month foreign asset disclosure scheme proposed in the Union Budget 2026-27, a young professional (category A) declares an undisclosed overseas asset with a fair market value of ₹80 lakh. Another taxpayer (category B) had paid tax on overseas income but failed to declare a ₹3 crore asset. What do they pay?

options.text: A: ₹48 lakh (30% tax + 30% additional tax); B: a fee of ₹1 lakh

solution.explanation: Category A (undisclosed income/asset up to ₹1 crore) pays 30% of FMV as tax and 30% as additional income tax in lieu of penalty: 0.6 × 80 = ₹48 lakh, with immunity from prosecution. Category B (asset up to ₹5 crore, income already taxed) pays a fee of ₹1 lakh for immunity from penalty and prosecution.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24 lakh omits the additional 30%; B does not pay a percentage of the asset; A is not the full FMV.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A: ₹48 lakh (30% tax + 30% additional tax); B: a fee of ₹1 lakh

fact_checks.claim: For category (A), the limit of undisclosed income/asset is up to 1 crore rupees; they need to pay 30 percent of Fair Market Value as tax and 30 percent as additional income tax in lieu of penalty; for category (B), asset value up to 5 crore rupees; immunity with payment of fee of 1 lakh rupees

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In February 2026, RBI proposed to allow commercial banks, subject to prudential safeguards, to lend to which entities that they had not been permitted to finance?

solution.explanation: Banks were not permitted to lend to REITs and InvITs at the outset; lending to InvITs was later allowed. In February 2026 RBI proposed to permit lending to listed REITs with safeguards and to harmonise InvIT norms.
solution.why_others_wrong: InvIT lending was already permitted; chit funds and Nidhis were not the subject.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI proposed in February 2026 to exempt certain 'Type I' NBFCs from the requirement of registration. Which?

options.text: Those not availing public funds and without customer interface, with asset size up to ₹1,000 crore

solution.concept: Ease of doing business for NBFCs
solution.explanation: Considering their low systemic risk, Type-I NBFCs—with no public funds and no customer interface—and asset size not exceeding ₹1,000 crore were proposed to be exempted from registration with RBI, subject to conditions.
steps: No public funds + no customer interface + assets ≤ ₹1,000 crore
solution.why_others_wrong: Deposit-takers, large-branch NBFCs and UL NBFCs are higher-risk categories.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Those not availing public funds and without customer interface, with asset size up to ₹1,000 crore

fact_checks.claim: Type-I NBFCs with asset size not exceeding ₹1,000 crore, may be exempted from registration requirement with the Reserve Bank subject to certain specified conditions

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: By a circular of 12 October 2026, RBI changed the rules for non-deliverable derivative contracts (NDDCs) involving INR offered by Authorised Dealers to non-residents. What is the new rule?

options.text: They may be offered to a non-resident user only for the purpose of hedging
They may be offered without any restriction on purpose
They may be offered only to residents

solution.explanation: Earlier, AD Category-I banks with an IFSC Banking Unit and SPDs could offer INR NDDCs to non-residents without restriction on purpose. Henceforth, they may offer them only for hedging.
solution.why_others_wrong: NDDCs were not banned or opened to residents; the purpose restriction was introduced, not removed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: They may be offered to a non-resident user only for the purpose of hedging

fact_checks.claim: Henceforth, Authorised Dealers shall offer NDDCs involving INR to a non-resident user only for the purpose of hedging

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following measures for urban co-operative banks announced by RBI in February 2026:
I. Raising the financial limits on unsecured loans and on loans to nominal members.
II. Removing tenor and moratorium requirements on housing loans given by Tier III and Tier IV UCBs.
III. Launching Mission SAKSHAM to train over 1.4 lakh participants from UCBs.
Which is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The Governor announced four UCB measures: higher limits on unsecured loans and on loans to nominal members (I), removal of tenor and moratorium requirements on housing loans by Tier III and IV UCBs (II), and Mission SAKSHAM to train over 1.4 lakh participants (III).
solution.why_others_wrong: All three are correct; the partial options omit one.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I, II and III

fact_checks.claim: The first two pertain to raising the financial limits on unsecured loans and loans to nominal members by UCBs; we also propose to remove the tenor and moratorium related requirements on housing loans given by Tier III and Tier IV UCBs; Mission-SAKSHAM intends to train over 1.4 lakh participants from UCBs

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about RBI's proposed revision of Kisan Credit Card guidelines (February 2026):
I. KCC tenure is to be extended to six years.
II. Drawing limits are to be aligned with the Scale of Finance for each crop season, with crop seasons standardised.
III. Expenses on technological interventions are to be excluded from the KCC limit.
Which is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The proposed guidelines include standardising crop seasons, extending KCC tenure to six years, aligning the drawing limit with the Scale of Finance for each crop season, and including (not excluding) expenses on technological interventions (III wrong).
solution.why_others_wrong: III is wrong; 'I only' omits II.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and II only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
RBI's circular of 12 October 2026 also required Authorised Dealers to keep a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR) on certain derivative contracts for their own hedging. Consider:
I. It applies to INR derivative contracts where the AD buys foreign currency against INR to hedge its own assets and liabilities.
II. The FERR equals 20% of the INR equivalent of the notional amount, kept in cash with RBI daily until the contract ends.
III. It applies also to contracts undertaken before the circular was issued.
Which is/are correct?

solution.explanation: ADs must maintain FERR on INR derivative contracts undertaken to hedge currency risk of their own assets and liabilities where they purchase foreign currency against INR (I), at 20% of the INR notional, in cash with RBI daily till termination (II). It applies only to contracts undertaken after the directions were issued (III wrong).
solution.why_others_wrong: III is wrong; 'I only' omits II.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: An Authorised Dealer shall maintain a FERR for foreign exchange derivative contracts involving INR undertaken by it for hedging the currency risk of its own assets and liabilities, where it is purchasing foreign currency against INR; FERR equal to 20 per cent of the INR equivalent of the notional amount, maintained by way of cash with the Reserve Bank on a daily basis until termination; applicable to contracts undertaken after the issuance of these Directions
